query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC high‐entropy alloys such as CrMnFeCoNi, pre‐engineering the grain boundaries by inducing controlled Cr‐rich nano‐precipitates promotes a shift in the crack‐tip evolution from intergranular decohesion to deformation‐induced local amorphization that forms energy‐dissipating nanobridges. This transition retards crack propagation and retains macroscale toughness under demanding loading conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy with conventional, unmodified grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat‐treatment and minor micro‐alloying process (e.g., slight Cr enrichment to pre‐form Cr‐rich nano‐precipitates) to modify grain boundary chemistry.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under representative aerospace loading conditions (e.g., intermediate to high strain rates and temperatures ranging from room temperature up to ~600°C) with similar grain sizes (microcrystalline to ultrafine).
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered grain boundaries enriched with Cr‐rich nano‐precipitates foster enhanced local amorphization at crack tips, leading to the formation of nanoscale amorphous bridges.
generation.mechanism: The pre‐formed nano‐precipitates at grain boundaries act as sinks for embrittling principal element segregation, improving local cohesion. Under high local stresses, these modified regions preferentially undergo a deformation‐induced crystalline-to‐amorphous transformation, forming nanobridges that dissipate strain energy and delay crack propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to unmodified samples, the GB‐engineered alloy will show a higher fracture toughness (e.g., increased KJIc) and a higher density of amorphous nanobridges at crack tips during in situ deformation. Cracks will propagate more slowly and with more tortuous paths, indicating effective shielding.
generation.baseline: An untreated CrMnFeCoNi alloy with standard homogeneous grain boundaries, which under similar testing conditions exhibits earlier intergranular decohesion and lower evidence of amorphous nanobridge formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for FCC‐structured high‐entropy alloys with similar grain sizes and chemical complexity, under conditions of moderate to high strain rates and temperatures up to ~600°C. Its applicability to HEAs with very different crystal structures (e.g., BCC) or under quasi-static deformation requires separate verification.
generation.uncertainty: While deformation‐induced amorphization leading to nanobridge formation has been observed (PMC8011962) and GB segregation engineering has been shown to mitigate embrittlement (PMC6897545), the quantitative interplay between these phenomena—especially given reports of nano‐precipitation reducing ductility in some cases (PMC11989734)—remains uncertain. Our hypothesis extends these findings by proposing that controlled GB engineering can tip the balance toward beneficial nanobridge formation rather than deleterious precipitate effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples: one set as a control (untreated) and another set subjected to a controlled heat‐treatment designed to produce a defined population of Cr‐rich nano‐precipitates at grain boundaries. Under identical high strain rate and intermediate temperature testing conditions, perform in situ TEM mechanical tests to monitor crack‐tip evolution and measure fracture toughness (KJIc). Complement these tests with APT or high-resolution TEM to quantify grain boundary chemistry and the density of amorphous nanobridges.
measurements: Fracture toughness (KJIc) through standardized mechanical tests
In situ TEM imaging of crack-tip regions to quantify amorphous nanobridge density and morphology
Grain boundary chemical composition via APT or high-resolution TEM
Crack propagation rate and path tortuosity analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the GB‐engineered samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in fracture toughness (e.g., higher KJIc) or do not demonstrate a higher density and effective morphology of amorphous nanobridges at crack tips relative to the control samples, the hypothesis that GB engineering enables enhanced toughness retention via amorphous nanobridge formation is falsified.
